title: Watching your first hockey game
summary: Follow the shape before trying to catch every touch.
points: Start with one player for a whole shift. Watch where he goes when he does not have the puck.
If the puck disappears, follow heads, sticks and the next receiver. The broadcast camera will not show every option.
For Montreal, begin with Suzuki (14), Caufield (13) and Hutson (48). Add more names as they become familiar.
tags: beginner basics first game Canadiens Montreal

title: Who does what on the ice?
summary: A normal lineup has five skaters and a goalie.
points: A centre supports through the middle and often takes faceoffs. Two wings provide outlets and attacking options.
Two defencemen retrieve pucks, protect dangerous space and begin attacks. They can join the rush when somebody covers behind them.
Five-on-five counts skaters, leaving out goalies. Positions describe responsibilities, not fixed patches of ice.
tags: positions centre center winger defense defence goalie six players

title: Why are they always changing players?
summary: Short, intense shifts make timing the change part of the game.
points: A shift is a continuous stint on the ice. Roughly forty to sixty seconds is common, with plenty of exceptions.
A puck placed deep can buy time for a safe line change. Judge the placement and the cover before dismissing it.
A tired group trapped defending may need a controlled exit more than another desperate clearance.
tags: shifts line changes substitutions bench tired

title: Offside in one minute
summary: The attacking blue line controls when players may enter.
points: In the ordinary case, the puck must enter the attacking zone before the attackers are fully across the blue line.
Skate position, possession and delayed-offside rules add exceptions. A frozen broadcast frame may not settle the call.
Offside concerns entry. Icing concerns an eligible long clearance; they are different rules.

title: Icing in one minute
summary: A long clearance can bring the faceoff right back to your end.
points: Broadly, icing involves an eligible untouched clearance from your side of centre beyond the other goal line.
Hybrid icing considers the race for the puck. Touches, playable pucks and other exceptions matter; shorthanded teams may normally ice it.
The territorial consequence and usual ban on a line change can leave a tired group defending again.

title: What changes when someone takes a penalty?
summary: Read the full set of calls before counting the advantage.
points: An ordinary minor is two minutes. A power-play goal generally ends a single minor that created the disadvantage.
A double minor has two segments. A major does not end simply because the other team scores.
Coincidental and overlapping penalties can change the arithmetic. A fight does not automatically create a power play.
tags: penalty power play minor major fight double minor עונש

title: What makes a power play dangerous?
summary: The extra player matters most when the defence has to move.
points: Look for a screen near the goalie, a threat between defenders and a receiver on the far side.
A lateral pass can force the goalie to move before the shot. An unthreatening outside shot may be easier than one more well-chosen pass.
Endless passing is not automatically good either. The defenders must have a reason to respect the next shot.
tags: power play PP special teams advantage screen יתרון מספרי

title: Spot a clean breakout
summary: The useful work often happens before the first pass.
points: Watch whether the retrieving defender checks over his shoulder and whether forwards come back to offer outlets.
A controlled exit creates an attack with several connected options. A clearance may only postpone the next defensive shift.
Judge the receiver’s options, not just whether the first pass was completed.
tags: breakout transition exit first pass support

title: What is a forecheck trying to do?
summary: Win possession back by guiding the opponent into a problem.
points: The first forechecker may steer the puck carrier rather than steal the puck immediately.
The second player anticipates the next pass; another forward often stays high enough to protect against a counterattack.
If everybody chases deep, one good outlet can beat the entire pressure. Watch the cover as well as the effort.
tags: forecheck pressure F1 F2 F3 dump chase לחץ

title: Was that goal the goalie’s fault?
summary: Start with visibility, lateral movement and second chances.
points: Could the goalie see the release, or was somebody screening him? Did a pass force him across the crease?
Was the goal the first shot, a deflection or an uncontested rebound? Defence and goaltending share the problem.
Save percentage and goals-against average need context. A few games can move either number dramatically.
tags: goalie save percentage rebound screen blame שוער

title: How do standings points work?
summary: Wins are worth two; overtime and shootout defeats are worth one.
points: A regulation loss earns zero. The third column in W–L–OT includes shootout losses.
Example: 20 wins, 10 regulation losses and 5 overtime losses means 35 games and 45 points.
Compare games played or points percentage before comparing raw points. Games in hand are opportunities, not points already won.
tags: standings points OTL record table W L OT נקודות

title: How does a team win the Cup?
summary: Qualify, then win four best-of-seven series.
points: Sixteen clubs qualify: the top three in each division, plus two wild cards in each conference.
Four wins take a best-of-seven series. The champion must win four rounds.
Regular-season overtime and playoff overtime differ. Playoff games continue through sudden-death periods without a shootout.
tags: playoffs cup best of seven bracket wild card overtime

title: Which stats should I start with?
summary: Learn what a number counts before deciding what it proves.
points: Points equal goals plus assists. Games played, time on ice and power-play opportunity help explain the total.
Shots on goal exclude misses and blocked attempts. Corsi and Fenwick count different sets of attempts.
Expected goals estimates chance quality with a model. Plus-minus is affected by many things besides a player’s own defending.
tags: stats analytics points assists goals Corsi Fenwick xG plus minus

title: Roster, lineup, scratch or injured?
summary: Four different ideas that are easy to mix up.
points: A roster is a broader list. A lineup is the group selected to dress for a particular game.
A healthy scratch is not selected despite no listed injury. An injured player may still appear on the roster.
Use the health page’s report date and an actual game-day lineup. Neither an old list nor a familiar name guarantees participation.
tags: lineup roster scratch injury availability IR

title: What does ‘day to day’ actually tell me?
summary: An availability label is not a return appointment.
points: Upper body, lower body and undisclosed are broad public descriptions; they do not establish a diagnosis.
Day to day and week to week are uncertain reporting labels. A historical injury is not evidence of a current absence.
Look for the date and the actual source. The guide records reported information and does not predict recovery.
tags: injury injuries day to day week to week health return פציעה

title: Drafts, contracts and the salary cap
summary: Teams balance tonight’s roster with a future one.
points: Draft picks provide rights to young players who may need years of development. A high pick is an opportunity, not a guarantee.
A cap hit is an accounting value and may differ from the cash paid that season. Injury relief has specific rules.
When judging a trade, ask what each side needs, what it gave up and when the return is likely to help.
tags: salary cap draft contract trade prospect rebuild AHL

title: Chirps, cellies and the television version
summary: Enjoy the slang without treating a comedy as a rulebook.
points: A chirp is a verbal jab, a celly a celebration and wheels a reference to skating speed.
Legal contact and dangerous fouls are different even when both look dramatic. An unnecessary penalty has a real cost.
You can ask a good hockey question without speaking in dressing-room slang.
tags: Letterkenny Shoresy chirp celly wheels slang culture

title: A two-minute game-watching plan
summary: One observation is enough to make the next game richer.
points: Before puck drop, check the actual starting goalie and significant lineup changes.
Choose one thing to follow: a player off the puck, support on exits or the weak-side receiver.
Afterward, save one repeatable strength, one recurring problem and one question for the next game.
tags: routine beginner game night notebook watching
